An interactive study of positron emission tomography

From decay
to voxel.

A PET scanner detects pairs of photons. From many such events, you infer where the tracer is. Start with the simplest question: how much can you see with fewer counts?

Phase 02 / Reconstruction lab

Measure. Predict. Update.

Reconstruct the same measurements with different algorithms. Switch a correction off to see what happens when the model leaves out part of the acquisition.

Corrections included in reconstruction

Loading the reconstruction engine…

—NRMSE to assigned activity‖x − xtrue‖₂ / ‖xtrue‖₂
—Poisson deviance / bin2Σ[ȳ − y + y ln(y/ȳ)] / bins
—Measured computation timeworker elapsed time · ms

The model used here

ȳ = A x + s + r
A = κ · diag(n · a) · P
aᵢ = exp(−Σⱼ μⱼ ℓᵢⱼ)
Pᵢⱼ = ℓᵢⱼ in cm

P uses Siddon intersections. κ sets the expected prompt-count budget; n is a prescribed efficiency pattern. Corrections alter A, s and r during reconstruction. The generated measurements stay fixed.

MLEM uses all angles for one update. OSEM partitions angles into interleaved subsets and uses a separate sensitivity for each. More subsets can accelerate early progress; they do not guarantee an equal wall-clock speed-up or monotonic full-data likelihood.

Numerical model, assumptions and verification

What is measured

The brain slice is averaged in 2 × 2 blocks from 128 × 128 to 64 × 64. The simulation uses 120 equally spaced angles over [0, π), with 129 bins at 2 mm spacing. Distances in the projector are in centimetres. This is a 2D parallel-beam simulation with no TOF, detector blur, positron range or PSF model.

All labelled head tissues use a water-equivalent μ = 0.096 cm⁻¹ at 511 keV. This includes the skull in this phase; it is not a calibrated bone μ-map. The cylinder has radius 80 mm. The point is one 4 × 4 mm voxel at (R, A) = (34, 22) mm, not an infinitesimal source.

Prescribed expected prompt fractions are T = 65%, S = 25%, R = 10%. Thus S/(T+S) = 27.78%. These are teaching inputs, not a scanner performance prediction. Scatter uses a broad Gaussian radial profile (σ = 64 mm) with 10% angular modulation; randoms are uniform. Both corrections use the exact simulated expectations and have no estimation uncertainty.

The efficiency is n = 1 + 0.15 cos(2φ) + 0.05 sin(2πb/129), with b the zero-based radial bin. κ = 0.65 N / Σ[n a P xtrue]. There is no decay or dead-time model yet.

What is reconstructed

x⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾ = x⁽ᵏ⁾ / (Aᵀ1)
　　　　· Aᵀ[y / (A x⁽ᵏ⁾ + s + r)]

MLEM and OSEM start uniformly in a circular support. Poisson measurements use a seeded product sampler below λ = 10 and transformed rejection above it. Turning noise off supplies the expected sinogram, which can contain fractional counts.

FBP subtracts the enabled additive terms and divides by the enabled multiplicative terms, then applies a spatial Ram-Lak filter and interpolated backprojection. Signed values are retained in calculations. The image display clips below 0 and above 7 a.u.; the caption reports negative pixels.

Post-filtering uses a Gaussian with σ = FWHM / √(8 ln 2), truncated at 3σ with zero boundary padding. It changes the displayed reconstruction and NRMSE; likelihood and deviance are measured before filtering.

Count sweeps run separate seeded acquisitions, not a cumulative event list. Turning corrections off preserves the same measured sinogram and exposure. All work runs in an embedded worker; the page remains self-contained.

Engine verification

Passed 15 checks covering ray lengths, projector adjoint consistency, point-source localisation, cylinder scale, attenuation, correction terms, Poisson sampling and worker cancellation. Noiseless cylinder mean: MLEM 0.9984, OSEM 0.9994, FBP 0.9996 a.u. (assigned: 1). Without attenuation correction: 0.1662 a.u. in the same central region. Point sinogram centroid error ≤ 1.00 mm; matched-projector adjoint relative error 3.9e-15.

Automated numerical and worker checks. Browser layout QA is still outstanding in this environment.

Phases 03–04 / From nuclear decay to image interpretation

Follow the physics into the image.

Change a parameter and follow its consequence. Chapters 1–6 share isotope, energy-window and timing settings. Chapters 7–10 add independent experiments in reconstruction, resolution, quantification and artifacts. They do not silently change the acquisition model in the reconstruction lab.

01 Decay02 Range03 Detection04 Coincidences05 Attenuation06 Time of flight07 Reconstruction08 Resolution09 Quantification10 Artifacts11 Your scans
01 / Radiotracers and decay

The isotope sets the clock.
The molecule sets the target.

In β⁺ decay, a proton becomes a neutron while a positron and an electron neutrino are emitted. The positron loses kinetic energy, then annihilates with an electron. In the dominant two-photon channel, each photon carries approximately 511 keV: the electron rest energy mₑc².

FDG follows glucose transport and phosphorylation; its retention is used to assess glucose metabolism. Amyloid ligands such as florbetapir bind to fibrillar amyloid-β. Sharing F-18 does not make these tracers measure the same biology. Deoxyglucose principle · florbetapir binding mechanism.

Physical decay reduces the number of radioactive nuclei. A decay correction refers measured activity back to a chosen time; it cannot replace counts that were never collected or undo biological clearance.

A(t) = A₀ · 2⁻ᵗ⁄ᵀ½
Acorrected(t) = A(t) · 2ᵗ⁄ᵀ½
Decays in window = ∫ A(t) dt

Specific activity is activity per mass, such as Bq/g. Molar activity is activity per amount, such as GBq/µmol. At the same activity, more non-radioactive compound means more injected mass and potentially more biological perturbation.

F-18, C-11 and Ga-68 half-lives are rounded teaching values from Conti & Eriksson; O-15 uses TUNL nuclear data; Rb-82 uses 75.45 s from NNDC evaluated nuclear data. The controls are simulation inputs, not dose recommendations.

02 / Positron range and non-collinearity

The annihilation is not exactly
where the decay happened.

The positron travels before annihilation. Its displacement depends on its energy and the material it travels through. Mean travel range and the FWHM of the resulting image blur are different quantities.

The two photon directions are also slightly non-collinear. A larger detector ring turns the same angular deviation into a larger position error.

Non-collinearity blur FWHM ≈ 0.0022 D
At the centre: blur ≈ D · δ / 4
δ ≈ 0.0088 rad ≈ 0.50° FWHM

Here δ is the deviation of the photon-pair angle from 180°. A 0.25° half-angle convention must not be labelled as that full pair-angle FWHM.

Effective range-blur widths and ring dependence: Moses (2011). Mean water ranges: Conti & Eriksson (2016). Ga-68 and Rb-82 means refer to their dominant positron branches.

03 / Photon detection

A crystal turns deposited energy
into a measurable pulse.

A photon may be absorbed photoelectrically or Compton-scatter in a crystal. If its full energy is eventually contained, it contributes to the photopeak. If a scattered photon escapes, only part of its energy is deposited.

For a 511 keV photon, a single Compton interaction can transfer at most about 341 keV to an electron. The corresponding backscattered photon retains about 170 keV. These are different energies, not competing definitions of the same edge.

E′ = E / [1 + (E/mₑc²)(1 − cosθ)]
Compton edge = 511 − 511/3 keV
Energy resolution = FWHM / Epeak

Scintillation light is converted to charge by a photosensor such as a SiPM. Integrating the signal estimates deposited energy; timing electronics estimate photon arrival time. A scintillator’s light-decay time is not its coincidence timing resolution.

In a multiplexed block, Anger logic estimates position from charge-weighted sensor coordinates: x̂ = Σqᵢxᵢ/Σqᵢ and ŷ = Σqᵢyᵢ/Σqᵢ. A calibrated flood map assigns that estimate to a crystal.

MaterialDensity (g/cm³)ZeffLight yield (photons/MeV)Decay (ns)Energy FWHM at 511 keV
LYSO7.16632,0004012%
BGO7.1759,00030020%
LaBr₃ (5% Ce)5.34760,0002510%

Historical example values: IAEA, Quality Assurance for PET and PET/CT Systems, Table 2 (2009). Composition, size and readout change performance; these are not intrinsic limits or specifications of current commercial scanners. Detector principles: Zatcepin & Ziegler (2023).

04 / Trues, scatter and randoms

More activity does not always
mean more useful information.

A true coincidence pairs two unscattered photons from one annihilation. A scattered coincidence includes a photon deflected in the object. A random coincidence pairs unrelated singles.

The random rate rises with both singles rates and the timing acceptance width. Narrowing the window rejects more randoms, but it must still accommodate photon flight-time differences and timing uncertainty.

W = 2τ (full timing acceptance width)
R ≈ W · S₁ · S₂ = 2τ S₁ S₂
Scatter fraction = S / (T + S)
NECR = T² / (T + S + 2R)

The 2R denominator here represents randoms estimated with an independent, equally noisy delayed window. A negligible-noise random estimate instead gives a +R term. NECR is a count-rate figure of merit, not a complete image-quality measure.

Activity here is present at scan time. It is separate from Chapter 1’s initial activity.

Inspect the count-rate assumptions

Let p and q be the accepted photopeak and body-tail fractions from Chapter 3. Two equivalent singles streams have Sin = 30,000 A (0.65p + 0.35q) s⁻¹, where A is in MBq. With an assumed paralyzable dead time of 40 ns, L = exp(−40 × 10⁻⁹ Sin). Rates are T = 1,500 A p²L², S = 2,000 A pqL² and R = W(SinL)², in s⁻¹. These coefficients and mixture weights are chosen teaching inputs, not fitted scanner parameters. True timing acceptance is assumed to be one throughout the available window range. No prompt-gamma or pile-up spectrum model is included.

Rate definitions and random estimation: IAEA PET/CT quality assurance. Do not use the displayed peak to choose a clinical injected activity.

05 / Attenuation

Both photons must survive
the entire line of response.

A photon that interacts before reaching the detector may no longer contribute to a true coincidence. For a uniform path, survival of the pair is the product of survival along the two opposing paths.

Ppair = e⁻µℓ¹ · e⁻µℓ² = e⁻µ(ℓ¹+ℓ²)
General case: Ppair = exp(−∫LOR μ dl)
Attenuation correction factor = 1/Ppair

Move the annihilation point. One photon travels farther and the other travels less, but the total path through the object stays the same. The unscattered-pair survival therefore does not depend on where along that LOR annihilation occurs.

CT measures attenuation at X-ray energies. A calibrated, often bilinear transformation maps HU to μ at 511 keV. Its bone slope depends on the acquisition and calibration; it is not a universal conversion.

MRI measures a different physical signal and provides no direct 511 keV μ-map. Tissue segmentation, specialised MR sequences and learned pseudo-CT/μ-maps bridge the gap. For a learned method, verify bone, air cavities, implants and out-of-distribution anatomy; a plausible image can still give biased PET quantification. An example of learned brain MR attenuation correction.

Water μ and CT scaling: Burger et al. (2002) and Carney et al. (2006).

The consequence in the embedded phantom

One fixed, noiseless acquisition. Thirty MLEM iterations; only attenuation modelling changes. These images use the embedded water-equivalent head and are independent of the slab and HU controls.

Preparing the matched reconstruction comparison…

06 / Time of flight

A timing difference narrows
where an event could have happened.

A timing offset places the centre of the event’s localisation kernel along the LOR. Timing resolution sets the width of that kernel. These are separate quantities.

x = c · (tleft − tright) / 2
Localisation FWHM Δx = c · CTR / 2
c = 0.299792458 mm/ps

With this sign convention, a positive delay places the event to the right. A 200 ps coincidence timing resolution gives a localisation FWHM of about 30 mm. It does not make the reconstructed image resolution 30 mm; many LORs constrain the image together.

For a roughly uniform object, a first estimate of effective sensitivity gain is D/Δx, with an SNR gain of its square root. D is the object diameter, not the scanner-ring diameter. This estimate is useful when Δx is smaller than the object.

Effective gain ≈ max(1, D/Δx)
SNR gain ≈ √(effective gain)

TOF localisation and approximate gain: Surti (2015). Exact reconstruction gains depend on the object, count level, timing model and algorithm; they are not guaranteed by this ratio.

07 / Reconstruction in depth

A model, an estimate, a correction.

Every update asks whether a proposed activity image could have produced the measured coincidences.

The system matrix is the bridge

For projection bin i and voxel j, Aij is the expected contribution per unit activity. Here Siddon’s ray intersections give the path length in each square voxel. Exposure, detector efficiency and the attenuation survival factor multiply each row. Scatter and randoms enter as additive expected counts b.

yᵢ ~ Poisson((Ax)ᵢ + bᵢ)
xⱼ ← xⱼ / (Aᵀ1)ⱼ · [Aᵀ(y / (Ax + b))]ⱼ

The transpose Aᵀ uses exactly the same path lengths as the forward projector. Sensitivity Aᵀ1 accounts for unequal sampling. In this notebook the matrix is stored sparsely; a ray only touches a small fraction of the image.

FBP, MLEM and OSEM

FBP corrects the projections, applies a ramp filter and backprojects. It is fast and linear; its ramp amplifies high spatial frequencies and noise, and negative estimates are possible.

MLEM uses all projections per update, preserves non-negativity and increases the Poisson likelihood for this matched model. More iterations recover detail but can amplify noise.

OSEM updates with interleaved angular subsets and their own sensitivity images. One pass through all subsets is one iteration. Faster initial progress does not guarantee full-data likelihood increases at every update; fixed subsets can approach a limit cycle.

03.57 a.u. · both images

Run the ensemble to measure the curves. Both images will use the same 0–7 a.u. scale.

Early stopping and regularisation

Early stopping and smoothing trade detail for lower noise. The graph estimates bias from the ensemble mean and spread about that mean; RMS error² = bias² + spread², all normalised by the truth’s squared norm. Eight samples give a noisy finite-ensemble estimate, not a universal optimum or an uncertainty interval.

x̂ = arg maxx ≥ 0 { log p(y | x) − β R(x) }

A penalty R can favour smoothness or preserve edges. Increasing β usually suppresses noise and can suppress true small structures too. Penalised likelihood is explained here; the lab itself implements unpenalised EM with an optional post-filter.

Resolution models and learned updates

A point-spread model can be placed inside A. Correct modelling may improve recovery; sharp boundaries, imperfect kernels and excessive iteration can produce edge overshoot. Inspect the PSF mismatch experiment in chapter 10.

FBSEM couples forward–backward splitting and EM with learned regularisation. TransEM embeds a residual Swin-transformer regulariser in iterative PET reconstruction. These research methods combine a measurement model with learned image information; results depend on training data, count level and evaluation task. Neither network is run by this notebook.

08 / Resolution & partial volume

A small focus cannot fill its image.

Separate the physical resolution budget from the loss of contrast when an object is small compared with that resolution.

An illustrative resolution budget

Combined FWHM
DOI / parallax contribution

FWHM ≈ 1.25 √[(d/2)² + r² + (0.0022 D)² + b² + p²]

Gaussian-equivalent quadrature inspired by Moses. Here d is crystal width, r effective range blur, D ring diameter, b = 2 mm assumed decoding blur. Our parallax proxy p converts uniform depth uncertainty (20 mm, or 3 mm with DOI) to FWHM using the obliquity angle. This is a radial teaching approximation, not a scanner performance specification. Settings are independent of chapters 1–6.

Recovering a hot sphere

Centre contrast recovery
Centre activity
Solid / blurred sphereDashed / true sphere

True sphere 7 a.u.; infinite background 1 a.u. An exact 3D ball convolved with an isotropic Gaussian gives the centre profile. Recovery = (blurred centre − background) / (true sphere − background). This is centre contrast recovery, not ROI-mean recovery, SUVpeak or a fitted scanner PSF.

Partial-volume effects include spill-out and spill-in. Object shape, background, motion, voxel sampling, reconstruction and ROI definition all matter. A recovery curve for one sphere model is not a general patient correction. Further reading: Soret, Bacharach & Buvat (2007).

09 / Noise & quantification

More counts. A steadier estimate.

Count statistics determine precision. Calibration, reference time and the choice of region determine what an uptake number means.

Synthetic phantom / same axial slice

03.57 a.u. · shared scale

Choose Run to compare the same axial slice. OSEM: 3 iterations × 20 subsets; 4 mm Gaussian post-filter; all corrections enabled.

Independent Poisson acquisitions with reproducible seeds, not subsets of one event stream. The ideal relative counting standard deviation is 1/√f. Reconstructed image noise is spatially correlated and depends on the algorithm. Linear dose–time interchangeability assumes unchanged physiology and count-rate performance; dead time, randoms, decay and motion break that approximation.

What does SUV divide out?

SUVbw = C(t) / [Anet(t) / W]
With kBq/mL, MBq and kg: SUV = C × W / A

Activity concentration and net administered activity must refer to the same decay reference time. Subtract residual activity and use the appropriate calibration. Body-weight SUV is conventionally reported as dimensionless under an approximate 1 g/mL density convention; the literal mass-normalised ratio has units g/mL.

SUVmean averages a defined ROI. SUVmax selects its hottest voxel and is especially sensitive to noise, voxel size and reconstruction. SUVpeak averages a small prescribed volume and is a different measurement.

SUVR divides target-region mean uptake by reference-region mean uptake from the same acquisition. Amyloid PET often uses a tracer- and protocol-specific cerebellar reference. Reference region, acquisition window and processing must be specified; a universal positivity cutoff is inappropriate. Example: florbetapir regional uptake study.

11 / Your scans · volume projection

Turn the volume in your hand.

A maximum-intensity projection (MIP) keeps the highest activity encountered along each sampled viewing ray. Rotate around the superior–inferior axis to see how structures overlap.

Projection of the embedded 3D activity volume, not a reconstruction from measured data. A 2 × 2 × 2 maximum pool produces a 64 × 64 × 48 grid at 4 mm spacing; rays are sampled every 2 mm using nearest voxels. Pooling preserves hot maxima but broadens small structures. This approximate MIP is for exploration, not quantification.

At 0°: R left, L right. Superior stays at the top. Other angles combine anatomical directions. Rotation starts only when requested and pauses when the tab is hidden.

Reference / Parameter trade-offs

Every gain comes with a condition.

Direction of effect under stated assumptions. These are design relationships, not acquisition prescriptions.

Read across for the benefit, its cost and the assumption behind it.
Parameter changePotential benefitCost or limitation
Injected activity ↑More true coincidences in the low count-rate regime.Greater radiation exposure; randoms and dead-time losses rise. More activity need not improve NECR beyond its peak.
Energy window narrowerRejects more scattered photons.Loses accepted true events too; the balance depends on energy resolution and object scatter.
Coincidence window narrowerFewer accidental pairs; R scales with the full window width for fixed singles rates.Can reject true events if narrower than timing uncertainty and geometric delays allow.
TOF timing FWHM ↓Better localisation along the LOR; approximate effective sensitivity gain D/Δx for a uniform object when Δx < D.Requires suitable detectors and electronics. TOF gain is task- and object-dependent, and is not a direct transverse-resolution improvement.
Crystal width ↓Finer spatial sampling and potentially better intrinsic resolution.More channels, cost and readout complexity; light collection, stopping power and packing also matter.
DOI information ↑Reduces uncertainty from oblique interactions, especially off-axis.Detector complexity and trade-offs in energy, timing or light collection depend on the design.
Axial field of view ↑More solid-angle coverage and more anatomy observed simultaneously. Integrated yield can grow approximately as L² for a uniform extended source in a short-scanner regime.Not a universal sensitivity law: ideal central-point geometric acceptance is L/√(D² + L²), which saturates. Attenuation, ring differences, source extent and bed coverage change the gain; longer systems need more detector material.
Scan time ↑More counts; ideal counting noise decreases as 1/√time for a stationary, constant-rate acquisition.Motion, radioactive decay and tracer kinetics limit the simple scaling; patient comfort and throughput matter.
Iterations / subsets ↑More updates can recover contrast sooner.More noise and potential edge artifacts. Subsets change convergence behaviour; equal iteration × subset products do not ensure identical images.
Post-filter FWHM ↑Smoother appearance and lower high-frequency noise.Reduced effective resolution and small-object contrast; SUVmax and partial-volume recovery change.
PSF modelling enabledMay improve resolution and contrast recovery with an appropriate model.Edge overshoot, spatially varying convergence and bias from mismatch. Reconstruction settings alter quantitative comparability.

L = active axial length; D = ring diameter. The central-point expression is an ideal open cylinder’s geometric solid-angle fraction, before attenuation and detector efficiency. The L² statement combines roughly linear local acceptance with linearly increasing illuminated source extent; it is a limited-regime derivation, not a fitted scanner specification.

Model notes / Sources

Built on explicit assumptions.

PHASE 5 · INSIDE THE SCANNER

Scope of this notebook

The embedded volume is an original analytic phantom. Ellipsoids, periodic folds and assigned tissue labels define its anatomy. GM : WM = 4 : 1, zero CSF activity and lesion activities are teaching inputs, not universal physiological ratios. Activity is in arbitrary units, not SUV.

The reconstruction lab uses one block-averaged axial slice and an ideal 2D parallel-beam geometry. Exact simulated attenuation, efficiency, scatter and randoms are available to the reconstruction. The main reconstruction lab has no scanner-specific calibration, Monte Carlo transport, TOF, PSF, motion, decay or 3D reconstruction. Separate experiments cover TOF, decay, motion and PSF mismatch. The rotating MIP projects assigned 3D activity; it does not add a 3D reconstruction model.

The count sweep now reconstructs noisy projections. Its relative counting-noise readout, √(10⁶/N), describes ideal count scaling relative to 10⁶ prompts; it is not a measured image-noise or NECR metric.

Numerical and worker checks cover the projection engine and teaching models. Phase 4 adds independent checks of sphere recovery, unit conversion, count levels, motion and correction mismatch. Phase 5 checks accepted event histories, cumulative Poisson counts, correction stages, timing units and Three.js scene construction. Browser visual QA remains outstanding.

Chapters 1–6 add independent teaching models for decay, range, detection, count rates, attenuation and TOF. Only the explicit “Try attenuation on/off in the lab” button changes reconstruction-lab settings. Chapters 7–11 add reconstruction statistics, partial-volume recovery, hypothetical SUV/SUVR, eight artifact modes and a rotating MIP. The four 3D scenes add recording formats, fullscreen and text fallbacks. Next: the final verification pass.

Primary references

  • Siddon (1985) — exact ray intersections with a voxel grid.
  • Shepp & Vardi (1982) — maximum-likelihood emission reconstruction.
  • Hudson & Larkin (1994) — ordered-subset EM.
  • Kak & Slaney, Principles of Computerized Tomographic Imaging — filtered backprojection.
  • Hörmann (1993) — transformed-rejection Poisson sampling.
  • NIST water attenuation tables — basis for the approximate water-equivalent μ.
  • IAEA Human Health Reports No. 9 — PET/CT counting statistics and image quality.
  • BrainWeb tissue-based models — background reading; not the source of this phantom.
